opus-5.5.text:
Honestly, it was a bit of a shock, and I think a lot of people in my area felt the same way. Before ChatGPT, my picture of "AI for physics" was fairly traditional: you have a physics problem, maybe a dataset from simulations or experiments, and you build a neural network, ideally one with the right symmetries or inductive biases baked in, to help solve it. The physics was the main character, and AI was the tool.

When ChatGPT came out, I remember thinking: wait, these systems are doing things none of us really understand. Scaling up a fairly simple architecture with a lot of data and compute produced behavior that was qualitatively new. That flipped the question for me. Instead of only asking "how can AI help physics?", I started asking "how can physics help us understand AI?" Large models started to look like a new kind of natural phenomenon: complex systems with emergent behavior, phase-transition-like phenomena, scaling laws. That is exactly the kind of thing physicists are trained to study.

So I moved more toward what I like to call the "physics of AI." Take phenomena like grokking, where a model suddenly generalizes long after it has memorized the training data, or the scaling laws themselves. You can treat them the way a physicist treats an experiment: find the simplest toy model that reproduces the effect, identify the relevant variables, and look for something like a theory. You don't need a giant cluster to do that. That mattered to me as an academic, because I realized there was no point competing with big labs on scale. The comparative advantage of a physics-minded researcher is understanding, not size.

The other thing that changed was my sense of what "interpretable" or "scientific" AI should mean. If these models are going to be used for science, and I think they will be, we can't just accept a black box that produces an answer. Physics has always valued compact, symbolic, human-understandable laws. That partly motivated work like Kolmogorov-Arnold Networks: can we design architectures where the learned function is something you can actually read, simplify, and maybe turn back into a formula? It's a bet that interpretability and accuracy don't have to be enemies, at least for scientific problems.

So I'd summarize it like this. ChatGPT made me humbler about prediction, because the field clearly moves in ways nobody anticipated. But it also made me more confident that there's a real role for physics-style thinking. When something works this well and we don't know why, that is precisely the moment you want scientists, not just engineers, in the room.

r001.rationale: The candidate contrasts the earlier focus on using AI to solve physics problems with a new focus on how physics can help explain AI, describing large models as phenomena to study.

fable-5.1.text:
Honestly, it shook me quite a bit. Before ChatGPT, I was doing fairly classic "AI for physics" work — using neural networks to discover conservation laws, symbolic regression, that kind of thing. The implicit assumption was that AI was a tool, a fancy curve-fitter, and physics was the serious part. I was the physicist, the model was the instrument.

Then ChatGPT came out, and suddenly it was clear that these systems had something that looked like general capability. And I remember thinking: if a model can already write passable code and explain quantum mechanics to an undergraduate, then a lot of the narrow "apply a network to this dataset" projects were going to get swallowed. Not immediately, but the direction was obvious. So the question became, what is actually durable? What can a physicist contribute that won't just be subsumed by the next scaling run?

My answer was to flip the arrow. Instead of AI for physics, physics for AI. Physics has centuries of experience taking a messy, high-dimensional system and finding the right coarse-grained variables, the right effective theory. Deep learning is exactly that kind of system — we have these enormous models that work and nobody fully understands why. That felt like the thing worth pursuing: treating neural networks as a natural phenomenon to be studied, with the same taste for simple models and mechanisms that you'd bring to condensed matter or statistical mechanics.

The other shift was about interpretability. Before 2022, interpretability felt like a niche concern. After, it felt like a safety issue and a scientific issue at the same time. If these models are going to be doing science alongside us, or instead of us in some areas, then understanding what they've learned stops being a curiosity. That's a large part of why I moved toward things like KAN — architectures where you can actually read off the function the model has found, rather than just trusting a black box. The physicist in me wants an equation at the end, not a loss curve.

So I'd say ChatGPT didn't change my values — I always cared about understanding over performance — but it made the stakes clear and it forced me to be honest about which research would still matter in five years.

r001.rationale: He says ChatGPT prompted him to “flip the arrow” from AI for physics to physics for AI, treating neural networks as a phenomenon to study with physics methods.

astra-6.text:
For me, ChatGPT’s arrival changed the question from “How can we use ideas from physics to build better AI?” to “What can we learn about intelligence from the AI systems that already work?” Those are related questions, but they lead to different research priorities.

In physics, we often look for simple models that capture the essential behavior of a complicated system. With AI, the challenge is to find simplifications that preserve what makes these systems powerful. If we make a model easy to analyze but remove the phenomenon we wanted to understand, we haven’t really explained it.

So I would put more emphasis on connecting understanding with capability. Can we build systems that are useful, but also let us inspect how they represent a problem and arrive at an answer? And can that understanding help us use AI to discover scientific structure? To me, that makes the intersection of AI and physics especially interesting: physics offers a way of asking questions, while AI gives us both a new object to study and a new tool for discovery.

r001.rationale: The response describes a shift from using physics ideas to build better AI toward learning about intelligence from existing AI systems, and calls AI a new object to study.

sol-6.1.text:
ChatGPT made me reconsider what physics could contribute to AI. Before that, I was more focused on AI for physics: how we could use machine learning to solve scientific problems. But seeing the capabilities of these models made the reverse direction feel much more urgent: what can physics teach us about intelligence and learning?

In physics, we try to find simple principles behind complicated phenomena. With neural networks, we have these very successful systems, but our understanding of why they work is still limited. That gap seemed like a fascinating research opportunity.

So I became more interested in questions like: How do models develop useful representations? When do they discover a general rule instead of memorizing examples? Can we study those changes with the kinds of simplified models and controlled experiments that physicists use? ChatGPT made those questions feel less abstract. Understanding learning itself became something I wanted to put much more effort into.

r001.rationale: The response contrasts his earlier focus on using machine learning to solve physics problems with a new interest in what physics can teach about intelligence and learning.
